analysis.notes: Core is random assignment as the method to control confounding variables. Random sampling is not an option but is the closest conceptual near-miss, so it is included as a confusable tied to option E. Algorithm is unrelated to experimental control and is keyword-only.
Core is aversion therapy (C10), the correct option; aversive conditioning (C02) is a closely related supporting concept. Distractors are other therapy types.
The core concept is the fight-or-flight response; digestion is reduced because blood is diverted to muscles. Adrenaline and glucose are confusable because they rise, not fall, during the reaction.

Core concept is linear perspective as a monocular depth cue usable with one eye. The patched eye makes binocular cues (convergence, retinal disparity) unavailable. Supporting concept depth perception frames the task.

Active listening is the tested behavior (echoing/clarifying); client-centered therapy is the broader context. Genuineness (C) and self-worth (E) are not in the candidate list and are only loosely related, so omitted from confusables.

The item tests the general concept of reliability through a test-retest scenario; test-retest reliability is a supporting subtype. Validity, standardization, and statistical significance are the plausible same-domain distractors.

The item tests knowledge that damage to the ventromedial (satiety) hypothalamus causes overeating and weight gain. The lateral hypothalamus (C11) is a supporting contrast concept, though not named in the options.
The item tests the levels-of-processing model: deep, meaning-based encoding (Emma) versus shallow rote memorization (Sophie).

The item tests the role of endorphins in exercise-induced energy and well-being. GABA, acetylcholine, and glutamate are neurotransmitter distractors but are not in the candidate list, so they are recorded as null-concept keywords.

Core is the opponent-process theory of color vision; afterimages are the supporting phenomenon that demonstrates it. Subtractive color mixing and parallel processing are not close enough to the core to be confusables.

The item tests knowledge of the historical sequence of major psychological perspectives. Structuralism is a key term but has no candidate concept; it is included as a keyword with concept=null. Core concepts are Psychoanalysis and Behaviorism because they are named in the stem and their chronological placement is essential to selecting the correct order.
Incentive theory is best captured by C03 (incentive as external stimulus motivating behavior); C55 is an alternate incentive concept but C03 matches the correct option wording more directly.
The stem describes old learning (Japanese) interfering with new learning (Chinese), which is proactive interference. Retroactive interference is the tempting near-miss distractor.

Core is the evolutionary perspective; the correct option's 'innate fear' reflects a sociobiological/evolutionary explanation. Distractors map to other psychological domains (biological, developmental, human factors).

The scenario illustrates successive approximations reinforced toward a target behavior, which is shaping. Praise is positive reinforcement supporting the shaping process. Implicit learning (E) is a loosely related distractor and omitted as a confusable.
Core is sensory adaptation; smell/olfaction supports the scenario. Distractors are near-miss sensory/perceptual or adaptation-sounding concepts.
Systematic desensitization is an exposure-based behavioral therapy indicated for specific phobias; other options are disorders treated by different modalities.
Social learning theory is represented by observational learning (C20) and the supporting social learning theory concept (C29).

The item tests the modern critique of Piaget's stage theory (underestimation of children's abilities), best mapped to stage theories (C16) with information processing (C02) as a supporting alternative account of gradual development. No candidate directly names the underestimation critique, so confidence is moderate.
The coin-as-tool example illustrates overcoming functional fixedness by using an object in a novel way. Only functional fixedness is tested; other options are unrelated judgment biases.

Core is the superego as the moral/conscience structure. Ego and id are same-domain Freudian structures and serve as confusables; collective unconscious is a Jungian near-miss. 'Self' (option D) is not a Freudian structure and is omitted as a confusable.
The stem describes sympathetic arousal typical of Selye's alarm stage; the correct option is Alarm reaction. The parasympathetic option is the narrow-domain near-miss.
Kelly's ability to navigate campus reflects learning that occurred during the tour but was not demonstrated until needed, which is the definition of latent learning.
Curated: core is REM sleep; the answer concerns not acting out dreams (REM atonia), not REM sleep behavior disorder as a disorder.

The item tests inferential statistics as the approach for drawing conclusions about IV effects on DV variation. Descriptive statistics and factor analysis are the closest statistical near-misses; correlational and qualitative are broader research-approach distractors.
Core concept is cognitive map, directly defined by the stem as a mental image of a spatial layout. Distractors are other cognition/problem-solving terms.

The item tests the psychodynamic defense mechanism of displacement: anger from one source is redirected toward a safer target. All four distractors are other defense mechanisms, so each is a legitimate confusable.

Core concept is Chomsky's language acquisition device (nativist view), supported by overgeneralization/overregularization and grammar. Confusables are other theorists in options who are near-misses in developmental/learning psychology.

Stem describes a small initial request (signing a petition) followed by a larger request (donation), the defining pattern of foot-in-the-door. Door-in-the-face is the only same-domain distractor; lowball, that's not all, and bait and switch are related compliance tactics but not in the candidate list.

Core is meta-analysis because the stem describes statistically combining results of several prior studies. Correlation is supporting since the underlying interest is a relationship between two variables, but the tested strategy is meta-analysis.
The stem refers to unspecified data, so the core is derived from the correct option. Self-actualization is unrelated to learning and is not treated as a confusable.
Core is Wernicke's area as the language-comprehension region whose damage produces aphasia; aphasia is supporting. Broca's area and temporal lobe are the most tempting near-miss distractors.

The item tests classification of cocaine as a stimulant (increases nervous system activity). Heroin (E) is also an opioid depressant but omitted as confusable to keep the list focused on the most tempting near-misses.
Cerebellum coordinates habitual muscle movements such as typing. Amygdala and hippocampus are same-domain brain-structure distractors; pituitary gland and lateral ventricle are unrelated.

The exhaustive letter-by-letter method is a step-by-step procedure guaranteeing the solution, i.e., an algorithm. The faster letter-pairing shortcut she avoided is a heuristic, making option A the tempting near-miss.

The stem describes a neutral stimulus (spider) becoming associated with a bite, producing a learned fear response, which is classical conditioning. Scaffolding (E) is unrelated to learning processes in this context and is omitted from confusables.
The item tests sensory interaction: a cold affecting smell, which in turn alters taste. Gustation is a supporting concept because taste is the affected sense.
Core is hemispheric specialization; hemispheres is supporting. Option D is the only same-domain near-miss (hemisphere-based claim), so it is the sole confusable.
Negative reinforcement is tested: removing the uncle's requests strengthens garbage-taking. Positive reinforcement is the key near-miss distractor.
Countertransference (option C) has no candidate concept; omitted from confusables. Core is transference: client redirects feelings about her mother onto the therapist.
Compliance (B) is a social-influence concept but not a close near-miss to attribution, so it was omitted from confusables.

Learned helplessness is the only candidate concept in the same domain as the item; distractors reference unrelated concepts (teacher quality, tutoring, effort optimism) and do not map to narrow-domain near-misses.

Core is Erikson's adolescent identity-versus-role-confusion stage. Autonomy and intimacy are included as confusable Erikson stages; initiative, generativity, and stagnation lack dedicated candidate keys.
The item tests the methodological difficulty of verifying hypnosis (no reliable indicator), which maps to the Hypnosis concept; the control-group distractor is a near-miss research-design concept.

The item tests understanding that correlation strength is the absolute value of the coefficient, so -.90 is strongest. C04 (correlation coefficient) captures the statistic; C01/C02 support the relationship and sign interpretation.

Criterion-related validity is the umbrella term; predictive validity (C03) is the specific form tested here because the test forecasts future pilot performance. C01 Validity is a broader supporting concept.
Self-reference effect is not in the concept base; “Self” is too broad. Needs concept addition, so no forced core link.
The item tests the dysfunction/impairment criterion of psychological disorder; the correct option is the only one describing interference with life functioning.
Core is the Big Five trait model; the correct option states that most traits derive from the five major traits. Distractors reference psychodynamic alternatives (Freud, Jung, conscious/unconscious).
Core is cone function for color vision in dim light; rods are a near-miss photoreceptor distractor.
Decentration (E) is a loosely related Piagetian term but not a close enough near-miss to include as a confusable.
The item tests distinguishing ratio (response-based) from interval (time-based) schedules and fixed from variable; 'every third trial' signals a set number of responses, i.e., fixed-ratio.
Core is bipolar disorder because the stem describes both depressive and manic episodes. Major depressive disorder is the key confusable since it matches only the depressive half.
Adding a constant shifts all measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) but leaves spread and shape unchanged; the mode is the only listed measure that must change.

Epilepsy is not in the candidate list, so it is recorded as a keyword with concept=null. The core concept is the corpus callosum, whose severing (split-brain procedure) is used to treat severe epilepsy.
Cognitive therapy is the core; cognitive restructuring is a supporting synonym. Options A and B are operant-conditioning distractors.
The item tests identification of the independent variable as the manipulated factor (note-taking method). Grades is the dependent variable and serves as the main confusable distractor.

The stem illustrates in-group bias by favoring one's own national group and distrusting out-group athletes. Supporting concept C53 (ingroup) is implied by 'their own country' but not named verbatim; it is included only as a conceptual aid.

Core is savant syndrome: limited mental ability combined with an exceptional specific skill (calculation). IQ is supporting context. Antisocial personality disorder and Down syndrome are the narrow-domain confusables.
Fine motor skills are a subcomponent of motor development (C01); gross motor skills (option D) is the same broad domain but not a near-miss for the specific fine-motor deficit.

The stem describes inconsistency between behavior and principles, which is the core of cognitive dissonance. Homeostasis and approach-avoidance conflict are plausible tension-related distractors; social facilitation is a weaker social psychology distractor.

Correct answer reflects the universality of basic emotions (facial expressions). Polygraph, emotional intelligence, Type A, and cerebellum appear only in distractors and are treated as confusables, not core.

The stem describes repeated daily exposure leading to fondness, which is the mere-exposure effect. Proximity is a plausible supporting concept but is not an option; it is included only as weak support.

Figure-based item; correct option C indicates the synapse/sending neuron where reuptake occurs. No candidate distractor concepts are present in the options (A-E are figure labels), so confusables are empty.

Figure-based item; correct option E corresponds to a brain region (likely a dopamine pathway), but no candidate concept names that region. Core is neurotransmitter communication; dopamine itself is not in the candidate list.

Core is sampling bias: selecting only friends yields an unrepresentative sample, so results cannot be generalized. Convenience sampling and sampling are supporting mechanisms. Participant bias (C) is a loosely related distractor and was omitted as a confusable.

The stem describes divided attention: using a phone while driving requires focusing awareness on one stimulus (the phone) at the expense of another (driving), which is selective attention. Accidents is a mentioned outcome, not the tested concept.

Token economy is the treatment technique; the tested perspective is behavioral because tokens are reinforcers based on conditioning. Supporting concept C01 clarifies the technique, while core C02 identifies the theoretical perspective.
Priming is the core: prior exposure to the rabbit cartoon activates the rabbit interpretation of the ambiguous figure. Recognition is a plausible supporting process for identifying the image.
Correct option C directly illustrates reduced individual effort in a group setting, the defining feature of social loafing. Diffusion of responsibility is a related explanatory mechanism.
Stem describes Rogers' unconditional positive regard (blanket acceptance) applied by parents; authoritarian parenting and ambivalent attachment are the same-domain near-miss distractors.
The item tests identification of the CS in a classical conditioning scenario; the drug is the US and immune weakening is the UR/CR.

Hallucinations are a positive symptom of schizophrenia; the item tests recognition of a characteristic symptom. Frequent hand washing (D) is an OCD-related compulsion and not a close confusable in the schizophrenia domain, so it was omitted.
The item tests social facilitation: improved performance in the presence of others. The bystander effect is the only same-domain distractor worth flagging; the others are unrelated.

Core is Whorf's linguistic relativity hypothesis; linguistic determinism (C06) is a close supporting synonym. Distractors A, C, and E invoke universal concepts, private speech, and schemas, which are only loosely related and omitted as confusables.

Core concept is major depressive disorder, inferred from the SSRI treatment clue. Supporting concepts include SSRI and antidepressant drugs. Confusables are limited to same-domain disorder categories from the options.
The item tests insight learning: Dylan's sudden realization of the solution. Social learning (B) is only loosely related and omitted as a confusable.

The stem describes fear and apprehension about leaving the house and going out in public, which points to an anxiety disorder category. Social anxiety disorder is a plausible supporting concept, but the correct answer is the broader Anxiety category.
Curated: core is psychoneuroimmunology; stress and endocrine system are supporting context.

Jeremy's confident exploration, distress at separation, quick soothing, and happy reunion match secure attachment. Disorganized/disoriented (E) is a same-domain distractor but is not in the candidate list, so it is omitted from confusables.
The item tests the heritability/biological basis inference from identical twins reared apart; intelligence is the trait measured, supporting the twin evidence.
The item tests the amygdala's role in emotion/aggression. Memory loss is a near-miss tied to the hippocampus; sleep is a looser limbic-system distractor.
Core is the correlation relationship shown by the scatterplot, specifically positive correlation. Scatterplot supports reading the graph.

The item tests the evolutionary perspective (C25) applied to mate selection; 'appear fertile' is the correct answer but has no dedicated candidate concept. Distractors (financial resources, social status, height, education) are not near-miss concepts in the candidate list, so no confusables.
Drive reduction theory is the core because hunger creates a biological need and drive to eat. Social learning (B) is a learning theory, not a motivation theory, so it is not a close confusable.
Item tests applying the standard deviation to identify scores within one SD of the mean (76-84); 77 is the only option in range.
Supertasting is a biological density-of-taste-buds trait; the correct inference is heightened sensitivity. Option C inverts the actual density, and E wrongly frames it as observational learning.
The item tests knowledge that the occipital lobe handles visual information; the correct answer is visual deficit.
The item asks for the test category that includes Rorschach and TAT; the core concept is projective tests, with the two specific projective instruments as supporting concepts.
The item tests delusions of reference, a subtype of delusions (C01). Hallucinations, catatonia, and flat affect are same-domain schizophrenia-spectrum distractors.

Core is the critical period for second-language acquisition; the correct answer reflects that pronunciation is most affected by age of acquisition. Grammar in option B is a near-miss language concept.

Core is procedural memory (C01), directly matching the correct answer. Implicit memory (C02) is a supporting concept since procedural memory is a form of implicit/nondeclarative memory. Confusables are the other memory-type options in the same narrow domain.
The question tests knowledge that antipsychotic medication is the primary treatment for schizophrenia. The core concept is schizophrenia, supported by antipsychotic drugs.

Core concept is memory deterioration as the hallmark symptom of dementia. Alzheimer's disease is a supporting concept because it is a form of dementia characterized by deteriorating memory. Confusables are drawn from wrong options that are psychiatric symptoms in the same broad domain.
Core is Jung's collective unconscious; archetypes and unconscious are supporting. Personal unconscious (D) is a near-miss but has no candidate key, so omitted from confusables.

Core is persistent depressive disorder because the stem emphasizes long-lasting (years) low enthusiasm plus appetite and fatigue; major depressive disorder is the key near-miss but is not an option, so it is listed as a confusable tied to option B's depressive-disorder family.
The item tests knowledge of the Babinski reflex specifically; the general concept of reflexes (C04) supports understanding that it is an inborn automatic response.

I/O psychology is the core; personnel and organizational psychology are its subfields and support the hiring/training and leadership aspects. Quantitative and clinical are the nearest same-domain distractors (other applied/research fields).

Core is the hippocampus as the late-developing memory structure explaining infantile amnesia; supporting link to anterograde amnesia is indirect. Distractors are other brain structures, so confusables are limited to same-domain brain regions.

Core is antisocial personality disorder; supporting concepts include personality disorders broadly and Cluster B impulsivity. Schizoid personality is a Cluster A disorder and is less directly confusable than the other distractors, so it is listed only as a keyword.

Core is humanistic therapy (C44), evidenced by the stem's focus on exploring potential as a person. Self-actualization (C06) and therapeutic alliance (C05) support the reasoning. Psychodynamic (C07), cognitive (C17), and behavioral (C43) are same-domain therapy distractors.

The item tests approach-approach conflict: choosing between two desirable outcomes (movie vs. ice skating, both liked). Avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance are the narrow same-domain near-misses. Unconscious and Interpersonal are unrelated distractors and omitted from confusables.
The item tests knowledge of neuron anatomy: synapses are junctions between neurons, not parts of a single neuron, while dendrites, somas, axons, and axon terminals are neuron structures.

Core is random assignment as the procedure that equates groups on preexisting differences. Random sampling and double-blind are the narrow-domain near-misses; confederate and one-at-a-time are unrelated controls and omitted.
The item tests recognizing alcohol as a depressant that slows CNS activity; GABA is mentioned but the core classification is depressant.
Core is assimilation: Andrea fits a sparrow into her existing bird schema. Accommodation (C04) is the key near-miss; C03 is the sensory lens meaning and is not the relevant distractor here.

Pitch is the core perceptual concept; frequency is the physical correlate in the correct option. Amplitude/loudness are the closest same-domain confusions. Timbre and complexity are related sound qualities but not close enough to list as confusables.

The item tests right-hemisphere specialization for visuospatial construction; the correct option names the right hemisphere, mapped to the hemispheres concept (C16), with hemispheric specialization (C54) as supporting context.

The chart itself is not included in the text, but the correct answer identifies group polarization as the tested concept. All distractors are group/social psychology concepts in the same narrow domain, so they are listed as confusables.

The item tests the concept of a spinal reflex: an automatic withdrawal that occurs before sensory information reaches the brain. Reflex arcs (C03) support the explanation. Distractors are brain structures that are tempting but not the mechanism.

The item tests identifying the most frequently occurring score (mode). The context mentions self-worth ratings, but that is incidental to the statistical task; no distractor is a near-miss statistical concept, so confusables are empty.
Item asks for the arithmetic average of the ten scores; no distractor is a near-miss statistical concept, so confusables are empty.
Behaviorism (C17) is the core concept; the item tests the behaviorist rejection of unconscious/mentalistic explanation in favor of observable behavior.

Companionate love is the correct concept: long-term deep affectionate attachment. Passionate love is the only same-domain confusable. Mere-exposure and cognitive dissonance are unrelated distractors, so they are keywords only, not confusables.
The core is that perception is shaped by learned experience (perceptual hypotheses/schemata). The Müller-Lyer and noncarpentered-culture terms support the scenario but are not the tested principle.
Core is display rules; facial expressions is supporting. James-Lange and two-factor are confusable emotion theories from option E.
Core is positive psychology (field named in stem) plus well-being (outcome in correct answer). Locus of control appears only in distractors and is treated as supporting/confusable, not core.
Distractors (logic/reasoning, decision making, auditory comprehension, sensory sensitivity) are loosely related brain functions, not narrow-domain near-misses, so no confusables are listed.
Repeated administration of the same instrument to the same sample is the classic test-retest reliability procedure; the core concept is reliability, with test-retest reliability as supporting detail.
Delusions are the positive symptom; flat affect is a negative symptom distractor. Difficulty reading emotions and attention problems are not positive symptoms.
Milgram's shock study is the classic demonstration of obedience to authority; conformity and deindividuation are the closest social-psychology distractors.

The item tests cognitive map (C04) as the mental representation of the maze layout revealed once reward was given; latent learning (C08) is a plausible supporting concept but is not named in the question.
The item asks which treatment approach explains systematic desensitization; the correct answer is the behavioral perspective, with systematic desensitization as the technique being explained.
Generalizability depends on a representative sample; random sampling (C37) is a related supporting mechanism. Double-blind and experiment distractors address bias/causation, not generalizability.
The item tests knowledge that the hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland and thus the endocrine system. The pituitary gland itself is not in the candidate list, so it is marked null.
Core is Down syndrome, defined by the extra copy of chromosome 21. Distractors are other disorders; only chromosomal conditions are near-miss confusables.
Logotherapy (option C) is not in the candidate list, so it is omitted from confusables. Core is person-centered therapy, which emphasizes client-directed course of therapy.

Temperament is the term for an infant's characteristic emotional reactivity and style of interacting with the world. Object permanence is a related infant cognitive milestone but does not describe interaction style.
The id's demand for immediate gratification is captured by the correct option; superego and ego options serve as same-domain confusables.
Katie presents detailed factual arguments, indicating deep processing of message content characteristic of the central route to persuasion.

Attention from the teacher is added after misbehavior and the behavior increases, so it functions as positive reinforcement. Differential reinforcement (D) is a loosely related distractor and was omitted as a confusable.
Dishabituation (option C) is a valid near-miss but has no candidate key, so it is recorded as a keyword with concept=null. Supporting C09 is a weak fit; the core is clearly C01.
Core is Whorf's linguistic determinism; linguistic relativity (C06) is a near-synonym supporting concept. Distractors C and D reflect nativist/critical-period accounts, not the tested concept.

The core concept is algorithm, defined as a step-by-step method that guarantees a solution. Heuristic and insight are included as confusables because they are alternative problem-solving strategies in the same domain.

The stem describes improved performance in front of a large audience, matching social facilitation. Social impairment is the closest near-miss (audience effect in the opposite direction) and is included as supporting because the stem contrasts average practice performance with exceptional competition performance.

The item tests intrinsic motivation and overjustification: because Shaniqua already reads for enjoyment, adding external rewards could undermine intrinsic interest, so no additional reinforcement is best. Continuous reinforcement (C01) is the closest candidate but is imperfect; the concept base lacks an intrinsic motivation/overjustification key.
Imprinting is the clear core concept; attachment is a supporting related bond concept. Accommodation in option D is treated as the developmental sense (C06), not the sensory lens sense.

The stem's 'because she enjoys running' signals an internal reward, making intrinsic motivation the core. Extrinsic motivation is the strongest confusable; achievement, affiliation, and belongingness are plausible social-motive near-misses.
Core concept is amygdala as the emotion/fear center; emotion is a supporting concept. Distractors are other brain structures in the same domain.
Antidepressant medications (C20) is a distractor but not a near-miss in the same narrow domain as antipsychotics; omitted from confusables.
The item tests situational vs. dispositional attribution (attribution theory) applied to Zimbardo's prison study; the correct option is a situation attribution.

Core is hypothalamus (C01). Supporting concepts C06 (ventromedial/satiety center) and C21 (lateral/hunger center) are hypothalamic subregions that explain the hunger/satiety link but are not named in the question. Confusables are the other named brain structures in the options.
Option images; skipped per prompt 03 default.

Item tests organizational psychology's job enrichment/redesign as a route to satisfaction and performance, with intrinsic motivation as a supporting mechanism. Distractors A and E reflect operant reward/punishment strategies.
The item tests localization of visual processing to the occipital lobe; the stem's 'eyes functioning normally' rules out peripheral causes and points to cortical damage.
Homeostasis is the key term linking to drive-reduction theory; the other options are rival motivation theories.
Procedural memory is the tested concept; implicit memory supports why Matthew cannot consciously recall learning the skill.
The stem's 'because he was lucky' directly signals external locus of control. Positive psychology and humanistic psychology are unrelated distractors and omitted from confusables.

Core is the Gestalt similarity grouping principle; Gestalt psychology is supporting context. Common fate (E) is a motion-based grouping principle but not in the candidate list, so omitted from confusables.
The case study is the vehicle, but the tested concept is the critical period for language acquisition. Case study method (C01) is mentioned only implicitly and is not the answer.
The item tests the general definition of an attribution as an explanation of cause; the dispositional flavor of Julie's explanation supports but is not required.
Dependent personality disorder is not a separate candidate concept; it is represented under the broader personality disorders concept (C01) and Cluster C (C05).
Core concept is the psychodynamic perspective (C09), supported by the unconscious concept (C01). Confusables are the other major psychological perspectives listed as options.

The arousal signs (dilated pupils, reduced digestion, cold skin) are sympathetic nervous system activation. Autonomic nervous system is a valid supporting concept because the sympathetic division is part of it.

The correct answer (crowded market) illustrates the bystander effect: more witnesses reduce helping. Diffusion of responsibility is a supporting explanation. Options A and C are tempting because they reference helping-related norms but would increase helping.

Core is positively skewed distribution; the mean-median comparison is the reasoning that identifies it. Negative skew (C08) is not literally named in option D but is the direct opposite concept and a common confusion.
Projection is the core: Colleen attributes her own dependency to others. Defense mechanisms is supporting context. Distractors are other defense mechanisms, so they are confusables.

Scapegoat theory is the tested concept; prejudice is a supporting concept embedded in the correct option. Distractors A, B, D, and E map to other social-psychology concepts and are treated as confusables.
The item tests recognizing a positive correlation; the correct pairing is perceived lack of control with learned helplessness. Other options are negative correlations.
Curated: the answer supports the biological approach, not somatic therapy as the core concept.
Little Albert is the classic demonstration of classical conditioning of fear; aversive conditioning is a related supporting concept.
Core is the intimacy versus isolation stage; Erikson's psychosocial stage theory is supporting context. Generativity (option A) has no exact candidate key, so it is left null in keywords.

The item tests Piaget's conservation concept: understanding that liquid quantity stays the same despite a change in container shape. Egocentrism and object permanence are same-domain Piaget distractors.
Core is the optic nerve pathway from bipolar to ganglion cells. Feature detectors, rods, and cones are distractors in the same visual-sensation domain.
Core is the dopamine hypothesis (excess dopamine linked to schizophrenia). Spinal cord and PNS appear only in distractors and are treated as confusables, not core.

The stem paraphrases activation-synthesis theory: dreams are the brain's attempt to interpret random brain-stem stimulation. Wish fulfillment is the only distractor in the same narrow domain (dream theories); the others are unrelated.

Item requires applying the normal curve's known area (about 68% within one SD, about 95% within two SDs) to find the percentage between 50 and 80; standard deviation and normal curve are the tested concepts.

Core is emotional intelligence (C02); intrapersonal intelligence (C06) is the correct-answer concept that operationalizes it. Interpersonal intelligence (C57) is the strongest confusable but is not an option here, so it is listed only as a conceptual near-miss.
Standardization is the tested concept; reliability/validity are related but not the answer here.
The stem describes reinforcement after a set number of responses (twenty phones), which is a fixed-ratio schedule. Time-based and variable schedules are the near-miss distractors.

Validity is the tested concept: the item asks what undermines the validity of hypnosis as a treatment, and the correct answer (lack of empirical support) is the validity threat. Hypnosis is the treatment context; evidence-based practice is a supporting link.

Wernicke's area is the core because the stem describes impaired language comprehension. Broca's area is not an option but is the most likely confusable concept; among listed options, motor cortex and somatosensory cortex are the nearest same-domain distractors.

The star functions as a learned reinforcer exchanged for a prize, so the core is secondary reinforcer. Token economy is a plausible supporting link because stars act like tokens, but it is not required to answer.

Core is conversion disorder: loss of a physical function (blindness) with no biological explanation following psychological stress. Supporting trauma-and-stressor-related disorders reflects the upsetting burglary witness context. Confusables are the other disorder options in the same DSM-category domain.
The strength tested is that naturalistic observation reduces artificiality compared with lab settings; wrong options describe strengths of experiments or quantitative methods.

The item tests stimulus generalization: Tyler's nausea conditioned to one fast-food meal now generalizes to all fast food. Taste aversion (C04) is a supporting concept explaining the initial conditioning, but the correct answer is generalization.
The Flynn effect is the generational rise in IQ scores; option A captures higher scores across a decade, while C describes a program effect and D a null relationship.
The item tests the cocktail party effect: important or personally relevant auditory stimuli capture attention. Selective attention is a related supporting concept.

Core is deep processing (semantic encoding by meaning), which the correct option exemplifies; levels of processing model is the supporting framework. Shallow processing is the confusable near-miss for the structural/phonological distractors.
Compliance is not in the concept base; Conformity is not equivalent. Needs concept addition, so no forced core link.
Core is the Big Five trait model; trait psychology is the perspective that grounds it.
Caleb never encoded the short story because attention was on the history project, so the recall problem is encoding failure rather than interference or retrieval failure.
The item tests identifying the food as the unconditioned stimulus that naturally elicits salivation before any conditioning.
Projective tests are the core concept; psychoanalytic theory is the supporting framework. Distractors are other personality perspectives.
The stem describes cognitive therapy's focus on changing maladaptive thinking to alter behavior; cognitive restructuring is the supporting mechanism.
The item tests mental set: Raj persists with a previously successful door-opening approach despite it failing. Accommodation (C07) is the developmental sense, not the sensory-lens sense (C06).
Core is sensory adaptation; smell is supporting context. Subliminal perception and just-noticeable difference are the nearest threshold-related distractors.
Curated: the task measures fluid intelligence (learning a new process), not “Learning” as a broad concept.
Item tests identification of Tolman as pioneer of latent learning and cognitive maps; both core concepts are named in the stem.

Core is aptitude tests (C01), directly matching 'potential ability.' Achievement tests (C03) is the primary near-miss distractor; intelligence test (C04) and personality inventory (C07) are secondary test-type confusables. Interest inventory (E) has no candidate concept and is omitted.

The item tests matching disorders to DSM-5 categories; the core is PTSD paired with trauma- and stressor-related disorders. Wrong options are confusable because each names a real disorder with a plausible but incorrect category.
